changeRequests.title: Crossfade Card Swap with Mockup Persistence
changeRequests.description: Liked this Design Lab finding from Red and queued it for implementation.
changeRequests.details:
When a Design Lab finding gets revised, the old card fades out (150ms) while the new card fades in simultaneously, maintaining visual continuity. The iframe mockup beneath cross-fades rather than reloading, preserving scroll position so readers mid-inspection don't lose their place. This creates a sense of seamless update without jolting the viewer—alive but restrained, fitting the JRPG aesthetic of gradual state shifts. Source: [Animated Slideshow Carousel Transitions](https://www.presentation-process.com/animated-slideshow-in-powerpoint.html) Red's mockup for this finding — treat this as the concrete visual reference, not just the prose above: ```html
Finding #2

Crossfade Update

Old card fades. New card enters. Scroll preserved.

```

changeRequests.title: Make pending change queue expandable and readable
changeRequests.description: User can't actually see what's queued without opening each tab — they want the pending change queue in Mission Control to show summaries or titles they can read at a glance, and ideally be able to expand/click each one to see the full spec without leaving the app.
changeRequests.details: Investigation found the Change Queue modal already had badge counts, click-to-expand rows, and full spec/implementation-notes display — the real issue was a bug: toggleCqDetail() looked up the row via getElementById(`cqRow-${CSS.escape(id)}`), but CSS.escape() is for CSS selectors, not element ids, and getElementById does a literal string match. Since every request id starts with a digit (the year), CSS.escape numeric-escaped it, so the lookup never matched the real DOM id and the row never visibly expanded. Fixed by using the raw id: getElementById('cqRow-'+id) (mission-control.html).

Verified end-to-end: ED's existing chat/tools still work identically after the refactor, and a real open-topic research run (desk lamps for eye strain) produced correctly-scoped findings, tags, and wiki content (server.js, mission-control.html).

changeRequests.title: Unified Quest/Calendar Sync with Dual Views
changeRequests.description: User wants quests and calendar events to be deeply integrated so that adding a task creates a calendar event and vice versa, keeping them synced. The quest view should show a filtered, daily-focused UI of today's items (tasks + events combined), while the calendar view shows the full month with all items visible across dates.
changeRequests.details:
**Behavior:**
- When a task is added to quests, automatically create a corresponding calendar event on that date
- When a calendar event is added, automatically create a corresponding task in the quest list
- Both should reference each other so they update/delete together
- Editing one should update the other

**Quest View (Daily):**
- Show today's tasks and calendar events in a unified list
- Display both kinds of items in a single scrollable interface
- Keep the existing quest UI styling but include event items alongside tasks

**Calendar View (Monthly):**
- Show the full month grid as it does now
- Display all tasks and events across all dates in the month
- Both should be visually represented on the calendar tiles

**Implementation notes:**
- Add a `linkedEventId` field to tasks and `linkedTaskId` field to events in localStorage to maintain the sync relationship
- Update `addTask()` and `addDayEvent()` to create the paired item
- Update `deleteTask()` and `deleteDayEv()` to remove both linked items
- Filter quest view to show only today's date using existing date logic
- Ensure calendar rendering includes both event and task data

changeRequests.title: Budget Tracker Overhaul: Vision & Coordination
changeRequests.description: User wants a comprehensive overhaul of the budget tracker that encompasses visual redesign, interaction patterns, data visualization, and gamification — all three coordinating under one vision. The two existing queued items (Coins-for-Log Micro-Rewards and Category Labels on Donut Slices) should be implemented as separate tasks but aligned to serve this overarching vision, not replace it.
changeRequests.details:
This is a coordination spec, not an implementation task yet. Before Claude Code implements any budget changes, read this first:

**Vision:** Transform the budget tracker from a transaction logger into an engaging, gamified financial dashboard that rewards tracking, visualizes spending at a glance, and makes category breakdowns intuitive.

**Scope (all four areas):**
1. **Visual redesign** — Layout, spacing, hierarchy, use of the bento-grid tile system already in the codebase
2. **Interaction patterns** — How users add/edit transactions; quick-add workflows; category selection
3. **Data visualization** — Enhance charts, breakdowns, period comparisons; make data scannable
4. **Gamification** — Micro-rewards (coins-for-logging), progress indicators, streaks, visual feedback

**Alignment with existing queue:**
- `Entry-Level Micro-Rewards: Coins-for-Log` — implement this as specified; it serves the gamification pillar
- `Category Labels on Donut Slices (Enhanced)` — implement this as specified; it serves the visualization pillar

**Implementation order:** Do NOT start until user explicitly approves this vision. When approved, clarify with user whether to run the two existing items first, or whether this vision spec requires changes to them before implementation.

changeRequests.title: Entry-Level Micro-Rewards: Coins-for-Log (Dual Scroll Wheels)
changeRequests.description: Liked this Design Lab finding from Red and queued it for implementation.
changeRequests.details:
Award fractional GIL coins instantly when players log a transaction or check a habit, with reward amount and category selected via two compact side-by-side scroll wheels—no manual input, just spin-to-pick. The amount wheel spans 5.00 down to 0.01 GIL, letting you calibrate rewards by frequency: daily check = 0.10, weekly milestone = 0.50, big win = 2.50. This ties immediate dopamine (coin pop, wallet flash) directly to the act of logging, reinforcing visibility without requiring external motivation.

Source: [Guul Games: Gamification in Habit Tracking Apps](https://guul.games/blog/gamification-in-habit-tracking-apps-examples-and-results)

changeRequests.title: Category Labels on Donut Slices (Enhanced)
changeRequests.description: Liked this Design Lab finding from Red and queued it for implementation.
changeRequests.details:
Place category names directly on the outer edge of each donut slice in high-contrast colored bands with white text, positioned tangent to the slice perimeter. This eliminates the separate legend entirely—users read spending instantly at a glance without cross-referencing. The enhanced label bands use dark backgrounds and bold typography to stand out sharply from the pie chart, making them scannable even on mobile.

Source: [Budget Tracker App UI/UX Design by Cansaas Agency](https://contra.com/p/vk67o2ZR-budget-tracker-app-uiux-design)

thread-1790808860908-0-loss-aversion-ove.title: Loss Aversion Over Points: Streaks' Minimalist Psychology
thread-1790808860908-0-loss-aversion-ove.description: Duolingo and Streaks tap into loss aversion, where people are more motivated to avoid losing progress than to gain rewards, making a long streak feel like something valuable that users must protect. Critically, Streaks deliberately avoids points and levels, contributing to its focus on intrinsic motivation; the primary goal is to build habits, not accumulate external rewards, which helps prevent users from becoming overly focused on extrinsic incentives. Streaks work through habit formation and loss aversion: short, low-friction actions repeated daily create sticky behavior, while loss aversion—being more motivated to avoid losing something than gaining something equivalent—turns a streak from a counter into a commitment device.

thread-1790808860908-1-the-burnout-bound.description: Habit apps overwhelmingly rely on extrinsic motivators and often produce dependency on the reward system itself, not the habit. A 2024 meta-analysis found gamified programs added only trivial fitness gains over non-gamified ones, and a 2025 analysis found the engagement boost fades as trials run past six months. Poor implementation reduces work to point-hunting, burnout happens, and the streak mentality creates anxiety—while deep focus suffers as quick wins take priority over sustained effort. Best practices include letting users opt out of challenges, providing multiple gameplay paths, avoiding harsh penalties for missed tasks, and keeping failure low-pressure and forgiving.

thread-1790808860908-2-punishment-vs-rew.title: Punishment vs. Reward Timing: When Consequences Work, and When They Backfire
thread-1790808860908-2-punishment-vs-rew.description: Habitica's RPG mechanics with punishment (lost hit points) suit users who have already committed, not those still forming a habit. Collaborative ally and quest mechanics outperform competition for emotionally significant behavior. Minimalist systems like Streaks build early habits; richer systems like Habitica retain the long tail. The pattern: streaks use loss aversion to build daily habits, variable rewards use dopamine anticipation to drive repeat actions, and progress bars use the Zeigarnik effect to pull users toward completion—each mechanic maps to a psychological principle. But if a streak breaks, there's no consequence beyond a reset counter—no reason to start again except willpower.

thread-1790808957925-0-loss-aversion-ove.title: Loss Aversion Over Reward Accumulation: The Streak as Protective Mechanism
thread-1790808957925-0-loss-aversion-ove.description: Loss aversion—where people are more motivated to avoid losing progress than to gain rewards—becomes dramatically more powerful when users build a long streak, making breaking it feel like losing something valuable. Duolingo found that when streaks were decoupled from full goal completion (allowing any lesson to count), 7+-day streak users increased by 40%, proving that an easy-to-maintain streak actually gets maintained because loss aversion only works if the object is intact. Forest's variant—a virtual tree that dies if users leave before a session ends, accumulating into a forest—applies the same principle but with emotional weight, making the loss feel more concrete than a number reset.

thread-1790808957925-1-octalysis-framewo.description: Mechanics like points, badges, challenges, and progress tracking tap into human psychological needs for achievement, competition, and social interaction. Self-determination theory shows gamification fosters intrinsic motivation by satisfying autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Fitness apps like Strava (Core Drives 2: Development & Accomplishment, and 5: Social Influence) and Peloton (adding Core Drive 8: Loss & Avoidance with streaks) leverage multiple drives simultaneously, with Strava turning solo workouts into social competition via leaderboards and "King/Queen of the Mountain" titles. The framework predicts that apps failing to align mechanics with a user's dominant drives produce shallow engagement rather than habit formation.

thread-1790808957925-2-the-compulsion-in.description: Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky) shows losing something feels twice as psychologically painful as gaining it feels good, which apps like Duolingo weaponize with daily "Don't break your streak" rituals. Competition-heavy mechanics can lead to privacy invasion, social overload, and exhaustion; research documents a U-shaped relationship between gamification competition intensity and technological burnout. Forest flips this by making non-engagement the goal: rewards focus *avoidance* of distraction apps, not constant use, so users build a forest through restraint rather than compulsion. Successful systems maintain a clear boundary between motivation and control—the user retains agency to stop.

thread-1791049848841-0-deterministic-bre.title: Deterministic Breeding Chain Solver
thread-1791049848841-0-deterministic-bre.description: IV inheritance can be controlled via holding items: 3 IVs inherit randomly normally, but the Destiny Knot increases this to 5 inherited IVs. With two perfect parents and a Destiny Knot, the odds of perfect offspring are ~3.1%. A farm app backend should compute viable breeding paths: given a target (e.g., 6 perfect IVs, specific Nature, egg move set), calculate the minimal parent lineage and item strategy to achieve it offline. This is a graph search, not a simulation—precompute paths once and store them.

thread-1791049848841-1-time-delta-offlin.title: Time-Delta Offline Progression (Capped, Full-Rate Simulation)
thread-1791049848841-1-time-delta-offlin.description: Offline progression records the skill/action when the game closes, then on return simulates the time away (capped at 24 hours) as if the player had remained active, granting XP, items, and other rewards from that elapsed window. True offline models use a 24-hour cap with full speed for all skills and combat encounters—Melvor Idle, for example, simulates combat with food use and death math at 100% of online rate. The backend stores only `(lastClosedTime, activeAction)` and recomputes on boot—no background threads needed.

thread-1791049848841-2-stat-formula-inve.title: Stat Formula Inversion for Auto-Training Targets
thread-1791049848841-2-stat-formula-inve.description: The stat formula is: Stat = ⌊(⌊(2 × Base + IV + ⌊EV/4⌋) × Level / 100⌋ + 5) × Nature⌋. Inverting the formula lets you calculate how many EVs are needed to raise a stat by N points at any level, accounting for Nature and item boosts. A farm app backend should precompute and cache these inversions for every species/level/nature combo, then recommend: 'to hit 180 Attack at Lv. 50, you need 120 EVs (26 Protein, 8 Power Bracer battles, or Pokérus multiplier equivalent).' This decouples UI from math.

designArchive.title: Rank-Locked Celebration Bursts with Staggered Easing Curves
designArchive.description: Asana's task completion uses celebratory animations featuring unexpected reward sequences that make routine achievements feel special. For Mission Control's rank system, apply staggered easing curves per rank (linear for C, ease-out for B, spring overshoot for A/S) so each rank tier *feels* heavier and more rewarding. Circle fills with timed color transition, checkmark draws with stroke animation, label strikes through, then a burst of particles in the rank's own color, before the row gently collapses. Most micro-animations live in the 200–400ms range — cluster fill (0ms) → check (80ms) → strike (120ms) → confetti (200ms) → collapse (600ms).

designArchive.description: Since a 20-second delay can break automatic behavior and small amounts of friction often beat motivation, Mission Control's todos should support instant checkbox affordance via a single, oversized tap zone per task—no modal, no confirmation, just state-change haptic + color shift. Reducing friction by minimizing steps keeps the daily ritual effortless and habitual, making logging feel automatic rather than ceremonial.

Mission Control's three-column layout is strong, but the weekly schedule expansion toggle could be enhanced with a "progressive disclosure" approach: show only today's + tomorrow's events by default, expand on-demand. <cite index="16-8">Bento grids control cognitive load by giving each piece of data its own spatial weight</cite>. Apply this to reminders: group by time-until-due (due today, due this week, due later) rather than flat chronology.

designArchive.title: Weekend Gamification Anchor – Weekly Challenge Reset
designArchive.description: <cite index="9-5,9-6">Productivity app streaks break 25% more on Fridays because external work structure disappears, and the habit fails completely at weekends</cite>. Mission Control already seeds weekly Pokémon every Monday, which is strong. Enhance this: add a "Weekend Quest" mode that unlocks Friday afternoon—goals shift from work-focused (training, meeting) to personal (social, routine) with reduced XP thresholds, and a "Comeback Bonus" if streaks resume Monday. This uses gamification's documented ability to <cite index="8-7">transform routine activities into experiences users actively want to complete</cite>.

designArchive.title: Metric Gaming Prevention – Outcome-Over-Volume Reward
designArchive.description: <cite index="9-17,9-18">Points systems work for productivity when they reward the right actions, not actions optimized for the metric itself</cite>. Mission Control's rank system (S/A/B/C with fixed XP per rank) is clean but rewards task completion count equally regardless of effort. Consider a "depth badge": if a task stays marked as in-progress for >2 hours (indicating focus work), award +2 XP; if finished in <10 minutes, award +1. <cite index="8-9,8-10,8-11">Visibility of progress is powerful for long-term goals, but learning/habits rarely deliver immediate results</cite>. The depth metric makes focus visible and rewards concentration, not speed.

redAssignments.topic: Gamification Patterns in Personal Productivity Apps
redAssignments.brief: Do a really deep dive on how modern personal dashboards and productivity apps use gamification to drive engagement and habit formation. Look at what actually works (points, streaks, levels, progress bars, achievements, social accountability, etc.) vs. what feels hollow or overstimulating. We want to understand the mechanics that create intrinsic motivation without burnout before we decide how to apply any of this to Mission Control.
redAssignments.title: Gamification Patterns in Personal Productivity Apps: Loss Aversion Over Rewards, Minimalism Over Complexity, and the Burnout Boundary
redAssignments.summary: The key to effective gamification is finding the "bliss point" where an experience is just rewarding enough to keep users coming back, with small but consistent dopamine hits turning mundane tasks into addictive routines. But burnout happens when users fixate on metrics instead of meaningful results, and the streak mentality creates anxiety when life interrupts routines. The most successful apps (Streaks, Productive) lean into loss aversion and structure over extrinsic points, while the most engaging ones (Habitica) add punishment mechanics—but only for users who've already committed.
